extracted.intended_audience: people interested in humor and the impact of popular and mass culture on society; professionals in communication and psychologists concerned with the creative process
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of a textbook that analyzes humor across media, genres and social dimensions, offering techniques, theoretical concerns, and case studies for interpreting jokes and comic texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider humor across everyday media
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor permeates every aspect of society and has done so for thousands of years. People experience it daily through television, newspapers, literature, and contact with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing humor, attend to how medium (TV, print, literature, interpersonal exchange) shapes form, delivery, audience expectations, and effects. Use examples from multiple media to illustrate cross-media similarities and differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of jokes as identity and social character markers
rubrics_metrics.description: The types of jokes a person enjoys contribute significantly to the definition of that person as well as to the character of a given society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat joke-preference as a diagnostic dimension: demographic, cultural, ideological, and social meanings can be inferred from which joke-types circulate in and define groups. Use this to evaluate social functions and implications of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of complexity in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: He shows how humor can range from the simple pun to complex plots in Elizabethan plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humor on a spectrum from simple linguistic devices (puns) to intricate narrative/comedic structures (plot-based comedy). Match analytic tools to complexity level (linguistic analysis for puns; narrative/theatrical analysis for plays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include ethnicity, race, gender, and politics as comic dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Berger examines a number of topics—ethnicity, race, gender, politics—each with its own comic dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly analyze how humor engages, reproduces, or critiques social hierarchies and identities. Use case studies (ethnic/racial jokes, gendered humor, political satire) to explore functions and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to multiplicity of ironies in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: He discerns a multiplicity of ironies that are intrinsic to the analysis of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for layered or multiple ironies within a comic text (verbal irony, situational irony, dramatic irony). Note how these layers interact to produce comic effect and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat apparently simple artifacts as complex and ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: He discovers as much complexity and ambiguity in a cartoon, such as Mickey Mouse, as he finds in an important piece of literature, such as Huckleberry Finn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss cartoons, comic strips, or seemingly simple jokes as trivial; analyze their ambiguity, historical context, symbolism, and narrative techniques with the same rigor applied to canonical literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider laughter's physical and mental health effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is beneficial to both our physical and mental health, according to Berger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include functional/emotional outcomes of humor in evaluations: therapeutic/healing applications, psychological benefits, and social bonding effects. Cite empirical or theoretical evidence where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a glossary of techniques: morphology of the joke-tale
rubrics_metrics.description: A Glossary of the Techniques of Humor: Morphology of the Joke-Tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a taxonomy or glossary of humor techniques (morphological elements of jokes/tales) when analyzing or constructing comic material; identify technique labels and show how they operate in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the anatomy/structure of a joke
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break jokes into structural components (setup, misdirection, punchline, timing, framing). Use structural analysis to explain how humor is generated and why certain audiences respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply theoretical concerns through case studies and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications (chapters apply analysis to ethnic/racial jokes, Jewish jokes, comics, popular culture figures, plays, novels, and therapeutic humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate analytic principles by applying them to diverse case studies (e.g., ethnic jokes, Mark Russell performances, Twelfth Night, Huckleberry Finn). Use application to test, refine, and illustrate theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore comedy's relation to creativity and creation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how the comic process intersects with creative processes: how humor is produced, the role of creativity in joke-making, and how comedic techniques foster or reflect creative thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider healing with humor as a distinct evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or crafting humor for therapeutic contexts, attend to intent, ethical boundaries, audience vulnerability, and measurable wellbeing outcomes. Distinguish entertainment humor from therapeutic humor in method and evaluation.
